baseProblem.statement: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The elements don't need to be contiguous.

rounds.question: What state tracks increasing subsequences efficiently?

options.rationale: A counter can't record WHICH subsequence endings are still extendable; you need the candidate tails themselves.

options.conceptLabel: A list of smallest tails by length
options.rationale: tails[k] holds the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1; keeping these minimal maximizes future extensions.
The O(n^2) DP works but is slower; the tails list with binary search gives O(n log n).

options.conceptLabel: A set of all seen values
options.rationale: Membership says nothing about increasing order or subsequence length.

rounds.question: With the tails list ready, how do you process the array?

options.rationale: Order matters for subsequences, so consume the elements in their given sequence.

fragments.java: int[] s = nums.clone(); Arrays.sort(s); for (int x : s) {

options.rationale: Sorting destroys the original order, so what you'd build isn't a subsequence of the input at all.

fragments.python:
for i in range(len(nums)):
            for j in range(i):
fragments.java: for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {

options.rationale: That's the O(n^2) approach; the tails method needs only a single pass with binary search.

fragments.java: for (int k = nums.length - 1; k >= 0; k--) { int x = nums[k];

options.rationale: Reversing turns an increasing search into a decreasing one, mismatching the tails invariant.

rounds.question: For each value x, where does it belong among the sorted tails?

options.conceptLabel: A linear scan for the first tail >= x

fragments.python: i = next((k for k, v in enumerate(tails) if v >= x), len(tails))
fragments.java: int i = 0; while (i < tails.size() && tails.get(i) < x) i++;

options.rationale: Correct result but O(n) per element; binary search on the sorted tails makes it O(log n).

options.conceptLabel: Always the end of the list
options.rationale: Always appending assumes every value extends the longest run, which over-counts non-increasing values.

options.conceptLabel: Binary search for the first tail >= x

fragments.java: int i = Collections.binarySearch(tails, x); if (i < 0) i = -(i + 1);

options.rationale: tails is sorted, so bisect_left finds the position whose tail x can improve (or the end, meaning x extends the LIS).

options.conceptLabel: Binary search for the first tail > x

fragments.java: int i = tails.size(); for (int k = 0; k < tails.size(); k++) if (tails.get(k) > x) { i = k; break; }

options.rationale: bisect_right skips an equal tail, treating equal values as increasing and overcounting for a STRICTLY increasing subsequence.

rounds.question: Given that position i in tails, what do you do with x?

options.conceptLabel: Append if at the end, else overwrite that tail

fragments.java: if (i == tails.size()) tails.add(x); else tails.set(i, x);

options.rationale: Reaching the end means x extends the longest run; otherwise x is a smaller tail for that length, improving future extensibility.
Appending unconditionally lets the list grow past the true LIS length on non-increasing input.

options.conceptLabel: Overwrite tails[i] without the end case
options.rationale: When i == len(tails) there's nothing to overwrite — an index error — and you never grow the list.
Inserting rather than replacing breaks the one-tail-per-length invariant and inflates the length.

rounds.question: Once every value is processed, what is the LIS length?

options.rationale: The tails list's length equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
That's a VALUE from the sequence, not the length you were asked for.
The final tail is a value, and not even necessarily the largest.
That's the whole array's size, an upper bound the LIS rarely reaches.

lightning.question: The tails-with-binary-search formulation — total time?
lightning.explanation: Each of the n elements does one binary search over tails (≤ n long) plus an O(1) append or replace — O(n log n), beating the O(n²) DP table.

lightning.question: [7, 7, 7, 7] returns 1. Which detail makes duplicates NOT extend the subsequence?
options: bisect_left lands ON the existing 7 and REPLACES it instead of appending — strictness preserved
Duplicates are filtered before the loop
lightning.explanation: bisect_left of an equal value returns that value's own slot, so equal elements overwrite in place and tails never grows. Switching to bisect_right is exactly how you'd get the NON-strict (longest non-decreasing) variant.

lightning.question: Follow-up: return the actual subsequence, not its length. What's wrong with just reading tails?
options: tails[i] is the smallest tail of ANY length-(i+1) increasing subsequence — its entries come from different chains, so you must record predecessors and backtrack
Reconstruction is impossible in O(n log n)
lightning.explanation: Replacements splice values from unrelated chains into tails. Store, per element, the index it landed at and its predecessor; after the scan, backtrack from the last length-L element. Same O(n log n).
